subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
passage: In the staff counselling room on the fifth floor, Kamal opened a small notebook and pushed it across the table. 'I did the homework.' Rukmini, the counsellor, smiled. Three weeks ago he had come in because his manager called him 'robotic' and his girlfriend, Neha, had said she felt alone with him. He'd said he had no idea what he felt, most days. Now the notebook held words for emotions, copied from a chart: irritated, disappointed, uneasy, proud. Each evening he had written one line. 'Tuesday: tight chest in the review meeting. Maybe… anxious?' 'Friday: warm when Neha laughed. Happy? Relieved?' Rukmini tapped the question marks. 'These are good. Guesses are how you learn.' Kamal almost smiled. 'It's like learning a language at twenty-five.'

qa.q: What did Kamal write for Tuesday?
qa.a: Tight chest in the review meeting, maybe anxious.

qa.q: What does Kamal's almost-smile at the end suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Kamal feels a small, shy pride and hope that the practice is working, even though it is hard.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini praise the question marks?
qa.a: Guessing a feeling from a body cue is the very skill being built, so rewarding guesses keeps Kamal trying instead of fearing wrong answers.

qa.q: How might Neha experience Kamal's growing words?
qa.a: Neha, who felt alone, may start to feel closer as Kamal can name moments like feeling warm when she laughed.

grounding: An adult who struggles to name feelings builds a word list and daily notes with a counsellor after problems at work and in love.

passage:
Dear Keerthana,
You asked what I've been up to since I stopped answering 'how are you' with 'fine.' Here's the honest version.
In January my boss said I seemed 'checked out,' and I realised I couldn't even tell her what I was feeling. So I started small. I printed a page of emotion words and stuck it inside my wardrobe door. Every night I write two lines: what my body did today, and which word might fit. 'Jaw clenched on the bus: annoyed?' 'Heavy shoulders after Amma's call: guilty? tired?'
In March, when it still felt tangled, I booked a counsellor. Best decision.
So, to answer your question properly: today I feel hopeful. And a little shy telling you this.
Love,
Ayesha

qa.q: Where did Ayesha stick the page of emotion words?
qa.a: Inside the wardrobe door.

qa.q: What is Ayesha feeling as the letter ends?
qa.a: Ayesha feels hopeful and a little shy, and quietly proud to name feelings honestly to Keerthana. 😊

qa.q: Why was booking a counsellor in March a wise choice?
qa.a: The feelings still felt tangled and had already affected work, so professional help added support beyond the word list.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel receiving such an open letter?
qa.a: Keerthana may feel moved and trusted, getting a real answer instead of "fine" for the first time.

grounding: An adult builds a feeling-word list and nightly body notes, and sees a counsellor when work suffers.

subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
passage: Chetan, you remember how Pooja left last year saying I was 'impossible to reach'? I thought she was being dramatic. Honestly, I didn't know what she meant. Then my team lead said the same thing at work, and I thought, okay, Saurabh, maybe it's you. So I tried something. I found a feelings chart online, the kind they give kids, and started checking it every night. Where's my body tight? Chest? Neck? Then I'd guess a word. First month, every answer was 'stressed.' Second month I found 'embarrassed,' 'lonely,' 'relieved.' In June I started seeing a counsellor every two weeks. Last week, when my sister had her baby, I told her, 'I'm so happy I could cry.' And I actually meant it. Knew I meant it.

qa.q: What was every answer in the first month?
qa.a: Stressed.

qa.q: Why does "Knew I meant it" matter so much to Saurabh?
qa.a: It shows Saurabh finally recognised and trusted a feeling from the inside, rather than just saying words.

qa.q: Which of Saurabh's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Checking body tightness each night and guessing a word built the skill slowly, and the counsellor added support once it mattered for work and love.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's sister feel hearing "I'm so happy I could cry"?
qa.a: Saurabh's sister would likely be touched and surprised, hearing such warmth from someone who rarely put feelings into words.

grounding: A young adult uses a feelings chart and body checks, then a counsellor, after hearing at work and in love that they're hard to reach.

subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
passage:
I'm Parveen. I sit across from Ujjwal at the bank branch, and this spring I noticed changes.
First there was a sticky note on the side of his monitor, a list of words in tiny writing: annoyed, let down, uneasy, relieved, left out. When he finished a hard call, I'd see him glance at it.
Then, during a tense meeting with the regional manager, he put his hand flat on his chest for a moment, breathed, and wrote something in a small brown notebook. He writes in that notebook every day at lunch too, a few lines.
One evening, walking to the metro, he told me, "My fiancée said I'm hard to reach. I realised I couldn't tell her what I felt, even to myself. So I see a counsellor on Thursdays now."
I don't know what's in the notebook. But last week, when I said I was stressed, he said, "Uneasy or overwhelmed?" and actually listened to the answer.

qa.q: What words were on the sticky note on Ujjwal's monitor?
qa.a: Annoyed, let down, uneasy, relieved, left out.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's hand on his chest suggest he was feeling in the tense meeting?
qa.a: It suggests he felt tense or uneasy and was using the feeling in his chest as a clue, pausing to name it in his notebook.

qa.q: What choice set Ujjwal's changes in motion, and why does it matter?
qa.a: After his fiancée said he was hard to reach, he chose to see a counsellor and practise with a word list and notebook, turning a hurt into steady learning.

qa.q: How has Ujjwal's effort affected Parveen?
qa.a: Parveen now gets a colleague who asks 'uneasy or overwhelmed?' and listens, so Parveen feels more understood at work.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, an adult who builds a list of feeling words, notices body cues, writes daily notes and sees a counsellor because the difficulty was hurting his relationship.

subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
passage:
Week one. Jahnavi, his sister, had asked Akash why he never said how he felt, and he couldn't answer. So he downloaded a feelings chart and stuck it inside his wardrobe. Most words looked the same to him. The only thing he could write in his phone notes that night was: "Chest tight before meeting."
Week three. At his second session, the counsellor asked what the tight chest might be. Akash stared at the chart printout. "Nervous? No. Scared I'll look stupid." He was surprised by how right it felt.
Week seven. Sunday lunch at their parents' flat. Everyone was planning Jahnavi's engagement, and nobody had asked him anything. Akash put his fork down. "I feel left out," he said. "I'd like to help with something."
Jahnavi stared at him, then grinned. "Who are you, and what have you done with my brother?" She handed him the guest list.

qa.q: Where did Akash stick the feelings chart?
qa.a: He stuck it inside his wardrobe.

qa.q: Why was Akash surprised in week three?
qa.a: He was surprised because naming the tight chest as being scared he'll look stupid felt so right, after weeks when all the words looked the same.

qa.q: What was the turning point at Sunday lunch, and how did it change things?
qa.a: Akash chose to say 'I feel left out' and ask to help, instead of staying silent, and Jahnavi responded by giving him the guest list.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see the change in her brother?
qa.a: She is surprised and pleased, and her joke shows that hearing him name a feeling is new and welcome after she once asked why he never did.

grounding: It shows an adult who learns feeling words over weeks with a chart, notes on body cues and a counsellor, until he can say what he feels to his family.
